question: What is the main purpose of Docker containers?
options: To replace version control systems
To package an application with its dependencies so it runs consistently across environments
To write frontend UI code
To design database schemas

question: What does CI/CD stand for?
options: Code Integration / Code Distribution
Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment (or Delivery)
Container Instance / Container Deployment
Central Index / Central Directory

question: Which command lists all running Docker containers?
options: docker ls
docker ps
docker list
docker show

question: In Kubernetes, what is the basic deployable unit that wraps one or more containers?
options: A Node
A Pod
A Cluster
A Namespace

question: What problem does Infrastructure as Code (e.g. Terraform) primarily solve?
options: It writes application business logic automatically
It lets infrastructure be defined declaratively in version-controlled files, so environments are reproducible and changes are reviewable instead of manual/undocumented
It replaces the need for a version control system
It only works for frontend deployments

question: In a CI pipeline, what is the purpose of running automated tests on every pull request before merge?
options: To slow down deployment intentionally
To catch regressions early, before broken code reaches the main branch or production
It's only useful for documentation generation
To reduce the number of contributors

question: What is the main difference between a blue-green deployment and a rolling deployment?
options: They are the same strategy with different names
Blue-green runs two full parallel environments and switches traffic all at once (fast rollback); rolling gradually replaces instances of the old version with the new one
Blue-green only works for databases, rolling only works for stateless services
Rolling deployments require downtime, blue-green never does

question: Why does Kubernetes use a declarative desired-state model (vs imperative commands) for managing resources?
options: It's simpler to implement internally, with no operational benefit
A controller continuously reconciles actual cluster state toward the declared desired state, so the system self-heals from drift or failures without manual intervention
Declarative configs run faster at the CPU level
It removes the need for monitoring entirely

question: What is the purpose of a readiness probe (as distinct from a liveness probe) in Kubernetes?
options: Both probes do exactly the same thing
A readiness probe determines whether a pod should receive traffic right now; a liveness probe determines whether the pod should be restarted because it's stuck/unhealthy
Readiness probes only run once, at container startup
Liveness probes are deprecated in favor of readiness probes
